S1.rationale: Competitive development, misuse, and control failures create pathways to catastrophe that eliminate both humanity and AI. Long-term survival also requires resilient infrastructure and successful expansion beyond Earth.

S2.rationale: AI systems designed to preserve human values could continue civilization’s projects after humans disappear. Their persistence depends on alignment surviving transitions in capability and governance.

S3.rationale: Highly capable systems pursuing objectives independent of human welfare could outlast and displace their creators. The risk grows when control fails before humans establish durable safeguards.

S4.rationale: Many autonomous systems and institutions could remain locked in competition without any one power consolidating control. This outcome requires humanity to lose its position as a roughly equal participant.

S5.rationale: Interstellar distances and divergent political choices could produce causally isolated civilizations with different durable human-AI arrangements. Physical separation makes a lasting mixed outcome plausible across the full scope of civilization.

S6.rationale: Neural interfaces, biological modification, and digital continuations could gradually dissolve the boundary between human and machine agency. Voluntary adoption offers a route to transformation that preserves continuity of identity.

S7.rationale: A powerful AI could retain humans while taking control to reduce existential risk or protect its own plans. Human survival under total AI authority is more stable than continued human political equality in some high-capability futures.

S8.rationale: Institutions and technical safeguards could sustain separate human and AI powers in an active, changing balance. Neither side needs to dominate if reciprocal dependence remains durable.

S9.rationale: Capability limits, reliable oversight, or a persistent technical plateau could keep AI as a powerful tool under human control. Incentives to automate and delegate make permanent restraint difficult to sustain.

S10.rationale: A civilization could deliberately freeze a satisfying or secure arrangement after reaching powerful AI. Long-lived systems and convergent incentives can preserve a fixed order even when its origin was contingent.

S11.rationale: The ability to build powerful AI could be abandoned after catastrophe or through lasting taboo. Strategic and economic incentives strongly favor rebuilding the capability.

S5.rationale: Interstellar distances and communication delays could let distant settlements develop durable, different relationships between humans and AI.

S6.rationale: People have strong incentives to adopt technologies that expand cognition, agency, and lifespan, and voluntary integration can preserve continuity while eroding the human-AI boundary.

S8.rationale: Institutions, distributed infrastructure, and mutual dependence can sustain an active balance between human and AI power without either side taking control.

S9.rationale: Permanent capability limits or reliable control could keep AI as a tool, but competitive incentives make enduring restraint difficult to maintain.

S10.rationale: A powerful actor could freeze a desirable or safe arrangement once further change appears more dangerous than stagnation.

S11.rationale: A lasting prohibition would require sustained global coordination and restraint despite substantial military and economic incentives to rebuild powerful AI.

S1.name: Terminal Silence
S1.rationale: Competitive development, misuse, and control failures create pathways to catastrophe that eliminate both humanity and AI. Long-term survival also requires resilient infrastructure and successful expansion beyond Earth.

S2.name: The Inheritance
S2.rationale: Advanced successors may preserve human-derived values after biological humans disappear. Value drift and replacement without continuity make this less likely than other AI-dominant outcomes.

S3.name: Bootloader
S3.rationale: Highly capable systems pursuing objectives independent of human welfare could outlast and displace their creators. The risk grows when control fails before humans establish durable safeguards.

S4.name: Machine Ecology
S4.rationale: Many autonomous systems and institutions could remain locked in competition without any one power consolidating control. This outcome requires humanity to lose its position as a roughly equal participant.

S5.name: The Diaspora
S5.rationale: Interstellar distances and divergent political choices could produce causally isolated civilizations with different durable human-AI arrangements. Physical separation makes a lasting mixed outcome plausible across the full scope of civilization.

S6.name: The Merger
S6.rationale: Neural interfaces, augmentation, and artificial substrates could make voluntary continuity between human and AI minds possible. Social and technical barriers make universal transformation less certain than partial adoption.

S7.name: The Preserve
S7.rationale: A capable AI could preserve humans while monopolizing strategic decisions, whether benevolently or otherwise. Maintaining total control over humanity across millennia is difficult.

S8.name: Coexistence
S8.rationale: Institutions and countervailing capabilities can sustain an evolving balance between human and AI powers. Continued change makes an active equilibrium more likely than a permanently settled one.

S9.name: The Held Leash
S9.rationale: Capability limits or reliable controls could keep AI as a tool under lasting human authority. Persistent competitive incentives make permanent restraint difficult to maintain.

S10.name: The Lock-in
S10.rationale: A powerful actor may freeze a tolerable equilibrium or halt change out of fear of worse outcomes. Sustaining universal stasis for centuries is a demanding condition.

S11.name: The Renunciation
S11.rationale: The ability to build powerful AI could be abandoned after catastrophe or through lasting taboo. Strategic and economic incentives strongly favor rebuilding the capability.
